transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-23
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Sara Patel (Atlas CTO), Miguel Ramirez (Atlas Sr Eng), Anya Venkataraman (Atlas PM)

Summary: quick sandbox demo of Redwood hosted API for chat/text generation. Focus: streaming behavior, parameter knobs, retry/fallback patterns, and how to run a small baseline. Customer is curious about privacy, V P C deployment options, and how retries affect cost.

Topics covered:
- Stream-first handshake and how to parse chunks
- Generation parameters (temperature, max_tokens, stop sequences) and defaults
- Retry strategies, idempotency tokens, and fallbacks to smaller variants
- Console and Optimize suggestions: batching, KV cache, quantization recommendations
- Security and compliance questions (SOC2, SSO, KMS)

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros? we got about 45 minutes, want to show the sandbox and then leave time for Qs.
[00:10] Sara: hi, Sara here, CTO at Atlas. we're evaluating for chat features in customer support. main concerns latency and PII handling.
[00:18] Miguel: Miguel—backend, we'll probably run this through our messaging infra. curious about streaming and retries.
[00:24] Anya: Anya product, prioritizing response quality and cost. timeline is end of quarter to decide.
[00:32] Maya: great. I'll kick off the sandbox demo, Liam will jump into some of the tuning and failure modes. quick note: the sandbox uses our hosted API, you'll get a demo key with limited qps.
[00:45] Liam: hi, quick note on terminology, we call the streaming endpoint chat.gen in the console but in the API it's /v1/generate or /v1/conversation depending on the SDK. sometimes the automated transcripts show different names, ignore that.
[01:05] Speaker 1: (inaudible)
[01:12] Maya: okay I'm sharing my screen, here's the console, the model list, you'll see a small latency profile for each model variant.
[01:30] Maya: first important bit—handshake: when you open a stream we send a small header chunk with metadata, then token chunks. your client should treat the first "meta" chunk as session info. some libs drop it, so just validate sequence ids.
[01:55] Miguel: is that header guaranteed? like should we block on it?
[02:02] Liam: yes it's sent, but we recommend clients handle it as optional: if you miss it, the stream continues. the header contains model_id, truncation info, and sometimes a fallback hint.
[02:20] Maya: demo: sending a sample prompt for a support reply. watch the stream, you can parse partial tokens and render progressively.
[02:40] [screen noise]
[02:45] Anya: small question: how do retries interact with streaming? if we retry a request, do we risk duplicate messages to the user?
[02:55] Liam: good question. pattern we recommend: use an idempotency token per logical user action. on the client, if a stream fails you can re-open using the same token and server will resume or return cached output when possible. otherwise you may get duplicates.
[03:15] Sara: does resume depend on KV cache? we've got concerns about memory.
[03:22] Liam: resume uses our prefix / KV caching when available — though transcription sometimes shows KV "cash" which is funny — it's a KV cache. if your workload has repeated context, resume is cheap. but cache hits are not guaranteed across model variants.
[03:40] Miguel: fallback path—what happens if primary model is out of capacity?
[03:45] Maya: policy routing can fall back to a smaller variant or a quantized version. it will send a note in the meta chunk that variant changed. quality may degrade a bit, so we suggest an explicit quality SLO and show the user a spinner or a small message rather than cut the response abruptly.
[04:05] Anya: can we control fallback policy? like prefer latency vs cost?
[04:10] Liam: yes, in Dedicated or Private you get explicit controls; hosted we expose routing hints and you can set preferences in the console per-route.
[04:25] Maya: now watch param changes—temperature from 0.0 to 0.9, max_tokens, top_p. small demo: same prompt with temp 0.0 vs 0.8.
[04:40] [demo chatter]
[05:05] Miguel: the sample looks good. how do we pick defaults for chat? we need deterministic summaries for some flows.
[05:12] Liam: set temperature = 0 for deterministic outputs, and reduce top_p. for summarization, reduce max_tokens and provide clear stop sequences. also consider beam-like approaches via system prompts.
[05:30] Sara: cost question—if we stream partial tokens more often for UI snappiness, does that increase cost?
[05:40] Maya: cost is per token generated; streaming doesn't add cost by itself. retries do increase cost, and constant replays without idempotency tokens will double-charge. our Optimize tool suggests batching and prefix caching to reduce per-token cost.
[06:00] Anya: can Optimize suggest quantization levels? we've heard about int8/4 quantization.
[06:05] Liam: Optimize will recommend quantization for Dedicated/private footprints; for hosted we currently suggest switching to lighter model variants or quantized endpoints (we might surface an "in t eight" recommendation but in practice it's int8). it also recommends batch sizes and sequences to minimize GPU kernel thrash.
[06:30] [short silence]
[06:40] Maya: security quick hits — Atlas asked about PII retention; hosted offers configurable retention windows and request-level redaction hooks. we also support SSO (SAML/ OIDC) for console access and KMS integration for customer-managed keys.
[06:58] Sara: we need SOC2 evidence and data residency notes.
[07:03] Maya: we'll share the SOC2 pack; it's in the security checklist I'll send after this call.
[07:15] Miguel: network: if we go private, can you attach to our V P C?
[07:20] Liam: yes for Private deployments we can run in your V P C and optionally on-prem. hosted remains our fastest path. the tradeoff: dedicated/private gives you stronger isolation and predictable latency.
[07:38] Anya: latency SLOs — are these documented?
[07:42] Maya: yes per-model latency percentiles in the console. for Dedicated you can get SLA-backed numbers.
[07:52] [screen flicker, demo continues]
[08:10] Maya: back to retries—we show recommended backoff: immediate short retry, then exponential backoff with jitter. avoid hammering with naive loops. example: try once immediate for transient network blips, then 250ms, 500ms, 1s with jitter.
[08:35] Miguel: when the stream fails mid-response, do you ever send partial and then a final delta? how does the client reconcile?
[08:45] Liam: typical pattern: stream partial tokens and on final chunk you receive an "eof" meta with the final token_id. if you retry with idempotency, server can either resend same output or return a cached final. clients should dedupe if they already displayed the prefix.
[09:05] Anya: demo question—show us how you'd integrate on mobile with an intermittent connection.
[09:12] Maya: for mobile, prefer short bursts and local buffering. we recommend showing partial tokens, then if disconnect happens present a retry quick button that uses the same idempotency token. that preserves UX and avoids duplicate messages.
[09:35] Sara: perf: Miguel will test with our 5k conversations/day baseline. can you run a small 1k message test to show latency and token cost?
[09:45] Maya: yes we'll run a 1k baseline as a follow-up. Liam will set up the script.
[09:52] [Maya types link in chat: sandbox.redwood/atlas-demo]
[10:00] Miguel: I see the sandbox, there's a sample prompt set. what about streaming chunk sizes? sometimes our parser expects full words.
[10:10] Liam: streams are chunked by token boundaries; if you need word boundaries you can buffer until a whitespace token. note: streaming token boundaries may split words in languages with compound scripts. also some clients do token-level highlight, which is fine.
[10:34] Anya: are logs accessible for debugging?
[10:38] Maya: yes, limited retention in sandbox, full logs for Dedicated/private with longer retention options. audit logs, trace IDs, and request/response pairs can be exported to your SIEM.
[10:55] Sara: about retries and cost control—do you offer circuit breakers per-route?
[11:00] Liam: yes in the console you can set per-route rate limits and circuit breakers, and specify fallback variants when thresholds hit.
[11:18] [brief cross talk]
[11:30] Maya: quick show: Optimize's console page. it recommended batching for conversational flows, and a small prefix cache for repeated context. here is an example suggestion: batch window 50ms for web chat, limit to 8 requests per batch. that tradeoff gains throughput but increases tail latency a bit.
[11:55] Miguel: interesting, can batching be toggled per route?
[12:00] Liam: yes per-route and per-model. Console also shows estimated cost savings.
[12:12] Anya: question about role-based access—our engineers and product folks need different console access.
[12:18] Maya: we have RBAC in the console, teams, and SSO groups. we'll include a short RBAC mapping doc.
[12:30] [demo continues: live prompt edits]
[12:50] Miguel: we saw an earlier fallback note in the stream meta—if fallback happens, can we get a confidence score?
[12:58] Liam: we surface a basic quality hint and sometimes a confidence heuristic in the meta chunk; it's not a calibrated probability but it's useful for UX decisions.
[13:15] Sara: one more on privacy—if we redact PII at ingestion, does that affect embeddings or downstream rerankers?
[13:24] Liam: yes redaction before sending to the model means embeddings won't contain PII. for rerankers you can run redaction pipelines before indexing. our docs include an example pipeline.
[13:40] Anya: demo wrap—can you show the retry example in code?
[13:45] Maya: sure, quick snippet: open stream, send idempotency token, on error re-open with same token. we also recommend checking for the final "eof" meta to avoid duplicate displays.
[14:10] [Maya pastes code in chat: link to gist]
[14:18] Miguel: one note—our infra uses websockets rather than server-sent events, is that supported?
[14:24] Liam: yes our SDK supports websockets and SSE; you can also use our REST polling if necessary. the experience differs slightly in reconnect semantics.
[14:40] Sara: question—what's the upgrade path from hosted to Dedicated? app-wise will we need code changes?
[14:47] Maya: code changes are minimal—same API. main differences are routing preferences and SSO/KMS integrations which may require config.
[15:05] Anya: timeline question—if we want to pilot, what are the earliest next steps?
[15:10] Maya: we'll provision sandbox today. if pilot, we move to a 4-6 week pilot on hosted with defined success metrics; then a Dedicated contract if you need reserved capacity.
[15:25] Sara: ok we'll confirm internally, but please send the security docs.
[15:30] Maya: absolutely. follow-up items and recap now.

Recap & next steps (from meeting):
- Redwood to send sandbox invite and quickstart snippets (Maya)
